opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the potential is very real, but it's arriving unevenly, and we need to be careful about where we say it's "accelerating" things versus where it's still mostly a promise.

Let me break it into a few layers. The first layer is what I'd call the infrastructure of mathematics: formalization, verification, literature search, routine lemmas. Here the progress has been striking. Proof assistants like Lean, combined with language models, are making it much cheaper to check arguments and to translate informal proofs into formal ones. That sounds unglamorous, but it matters. A huge amount of mathematicians' time goes into checking details, finding the right reference, or realizing that someone in a neighboring field already solved your sub-problem twenty years ago. If AI removes that friction, everyone moves faster, even if the AI itself never "discovers" anything.

The second layer is AI as a collaborator in exploration: suggesting conjectures, finding counterexamples, searching enormous combinatorial spaces, proposing constructions a human wouldn't think to try. We've seen genuine results there: new bounds, better constructions, patterns spotted in data that led humans to prove theorems. I'd say this is where the practical value is clearest right now. The model doesn't need to be a great mathematician. It needs to be tireless and willing to try a million ideas, and a human or a verifier filters the output.

The third layer is the one people get most excited about: AI independently producing deep, conceptually new mathematics, the kind that opens up a field. I think we're not there yet. Competition-level problem solving has improved dramatically, but research mathematics is different. Much of the difficulty is figuring out what the right question is and which definitions to make, and that kind of taste is still largely human.

Why does this matter for science more broadly? Mathematics is the bottleneck behind a lot of other things: physics, cryptography, optimization, verification of software and hardware, even the theory of machine learning itself. If AI lowers the cost of rigorous reasoning, the benefits spill over. Rigor is also exactly what makes AI outputs trustworthy. A proof that a machine has checked is trustworthy in a way a plausible-sounding paragraph isn't. So I see math as a uniquely good testbed for AI, and AI as a uniquely good amplifier for math.

My overall assessment is cautiously optimistic. In the near term, maybe the next few years, the biggest gains will come from AI making mathematicians and scientists more productive, not replacing them. The breakthroughs will mostly come from human-AI teams, and the bottleneck will increasingly be people who know how to ask good questions and set up the right verification loop. That's a real acceleration, even if it's less cinematic than "the AI proved the Riemann hypothesis."

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd split the answer into two parts, because "AI for math" means two quite different things right now, and people tend to blur them together.

The first part is formal verification and proof search, the Lean-style work. Here the progress is real and measurable. Models can now fill in routine lemmas, translate informal arguments into checkable code, and occasionally find a proof a human missed. That's genuinely useful, but mostly as infrastructure. It lowers the cost of being rigorous. It doesn't yet tell you which theorem is worth proving, and in research, choosing the question is most of the work.

The second part is the one that matters more for science, and it's where I'd be more cautious. The hard step in mathematics, and in physics or materials science, isn't manipulating symbols. It's forming the right abstraction. When I think about my own work, the breakthroughs came from a physical intuition about what the system should do, and the math followed. Today's models are very good at the "math follows" part. They're much weaker at the intuition part, because that intuition is usually built from failed experiments, from things that didn't work, and that data mostly isn't written down anywhere.

So my practical assessment is this. In the near term, AI will compress the time between having an idea and knowing whether it's correct. That alone could speed up fields where verification is the bottleneck, and there are many. What it won't do, at least not yet, is replace the slow process of a person staring at a confusing result until the right picture emerges. If anything, it will make that human judgment more valuable, because the cheap steps will be automated and the expensive steps will be all that's left.

One more thing I'd add. The biggest risk isn't that the tools are weak. It's that they're fluent, and fluency can look like understanding. A model will give you a confident derivation that's subtly wrong, and in science a subtle wrong is worse than an obvious one. So I think the people who benefit most will be those who use these systems as a very fast, very tireless collaborator, while still insisting on checking the physics themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is substantial, but we should distinguish between solving a mathematical problem and accelerating a scientific discovery. Those are related, but there are several steps in between.

Mathematics gives us a particularly useful setting for AI because, in principle, an argument can be checked rigorously. An AI might suggest a conjecture, find a useful example, or propose a proof. If we can then verify that proof, we have something much more reliable than a plausible-sounding answer. The challenge is that verification does not automatically tell us which questions are worth asking.

In science, that choice is often the hard part. You need to identify the right assumptions, decide what to simplify, and understand whether the mathematical result actually describes the physical system. A perfectly correct solution to the wrong model does not move the science forward.

So today, I would view AI primarily as a collaborator that can shorten parts of the research cycle: exploring possibilities, handling calculations, and helping researchers test ideas. That could have a very meaningful cumulative effect. But I would be cautious about equating performance on well-defined mathematics problems with an ability to make scientific breakthroughs independently. The practical test is whether it helps us reach a new, verifiable result faster, including the work needed to check its output.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we need to distinguish solving a mathematical problem from knowing which problem is worth solving. AI is making progress on the first, while the second still depends heavily on scientific judgment.

In mathematics, a plausible argument isn’t enough. One incorrect step can invalidate the whole proof. That makes systems that combine AI with formal verification especially interesting: the AI proposes an argument, and a proof checker verifies whether each step follows. The challenge is that translating a research question into a formal statement can itself take substantial work.

For science, though, useful results don’t always require a completely new theorem. Better algorithms, better approximations, or a clearer understanding of why a numerical method works can all accelerate research. AI could help explore examples, identify patterns, and suggest intermediate results that a researcher might otherwise spend weeks looking for.

So today I would view it as a tool for shortening parts of the research cycle. The important test is whether it helps scientists reach reliable, useful results faster—including the time spent checking its output. That’s a more meaningful measure than whether it can produce an impressive-looking solution.
